gloss_terse: to pluck off or pull out (twigs, ears of grain, plants); to be plucked
gloss_readable: A concrete agricultural verb describing the act of plucking or pulling off vegetation by hand. In Deuteronomy 23:25 it permits plucking ears of grain while passing through a neighbor's field, while in Ezekiel 17:4,22 it appears in the striking eagle allegory where God plucks a tender sprig from the cedar of Lebanon. The Spanish 'arrancar' (to uproot/tear off) and French 'couper' (to cut) capture the forceful manual action. Job 30:4 uses the participle for the destitute who pluck mallow for food.

senses.1: To pluck off or pull out vegetation—twigs, ears of grain, or plants—by hand. The cross-lingual glosses converge on manual removal: English 'pluck,' Spanish 'arrancar' (tear off), French 'couper' (cut). All five occurrences involve plant material: the eagle plucking cedar twigs (Ezek 17:4,22), gleaning grain (Deut 23:25), the destitute plucking mallow (Job 30:4), and the Niphal passive 'is plucked off' for a plant withering before harvest (Job 8:12).

gloss_terse: castor-oil plant, gourd (the fast-growing plant God appointed to shade Jonah)
gloss_readable: Found exclusively in Jonah 4:6–10, this noun denotes the fast-growing plant God prepared to shade the reluctant prophet, then destroyed with a worm. Its precise botanical identity has long been debated. The Spanish 'ricino' (castor plant) reflects the traditional rabbinic and Septuagint identification with Ricinus communis, known for its rapid growth in the Levantine climate. The narrative uses this plant to teach Jonah about divine compassion for Nineveh.

senses.1: A specific plant—most likely the castor-oil plant (Ricinus communis)—appointed by God to provide shade for Jonah. Spanish consistently renders 'ricino' / 'planta de ricino,' reflecting the ancient identification going back to Jerome and the Septuagint (κολοκύνθη in some manuscripts). All five occurrences cluster in Jonah 4:6–10, tracing the plant's miraculous growth, Jonah's delight in it, and its sudden destruction by a worm as a divine object lesson.

gloss_terse: to cut off, scrape off; to destroy or diminish (peoples, limbs, surfaces)
gloss_readable: A verb of severance and removal used across diverse contexts. In Leviticus 14:41,43 the Hiphil describes scraping plaster off the walls of a house suspected of 'leprosy'—a priestly purification procedure. In 2 Kings 10:32 God begins to 'cut off' portions of Israel through Hazael's raids. Habakkuk 2:10 condemns the one who gains by 'cutting off many peoples.' The figurative use in Proverbs 26:6 portrays the fool's messenger as one who 'cuts off the feet'—i.e., harms oneself. Spanish 'cortar' and French 'couper' consistently render the core cutting action.

senses.1: To cut off, scrape off, or remove by force—applied to surfaces, peoples, or limbs. The multilingual glosses uniformly cluster around cutting: Spanish 'cortar,' French 'couper,' English 'cuts off' / 'scraping.' The Hiphil in Leviticus 14:41,43 specializes as scraping house walls during ritual cleansing, while the Qal and Piel extend to destroying peoples (Hab 2:10; 2 Kgs 10:32) and the vivid metaphor of cutting off one's own feet by sending a message through a fool (Prov 26:6).

gloss_terse: end, limit; used in the phrase 'no end to' indicating boundlessness
gloss_readable: A noun meaning 'end' or 'limit,' appearing exclusively in the fixed phrase 'there is no end to' (אֵין קֵצֶה). Isaiah 2:7 uses it twice: there is no end to Judah's silver and gold, nor to their chariots—an ironic indictment of materialistic excess. Nahum deploys the same construction for Nineveh's plundered wealth (2:9), heaped corpses (3:3), and limitless strength (3:9). Spanish 'fin' and 'límite' along with French 'extrémité' confirm the spatial-quantitative sense of a boundary that does not exist.

senses.1: An end or limit, always negated in the phrase 'there is no end to,' expressing inexhaustible quantity or extent. Spanish 'fin' / 'límite' and French 'extrémité' converge on the boundary concept. Isaiah 2:7 pairs it twice for Judah's endless wealth and chariots, while Nahum applies it to Nineveh's bottomless plunder (2:9), innumerable corpses (3:3), and boundless military strength (3:9)—each time underscoring overwhelming, unchecked excess.

gloss_terse: bough(s), branch(es); collectively, the leafy growth of a tree (distinct from harvest homonym)
gloss_readable: Not to be confused with the common homonym meaning 'harvest,' this noun refers to the branches or boughs of a tree, typically used collectively. Job uses it three times in rich metaphorical language: roots and branches represent a person's total life (18:16; 29:19), and even a felled tree can sprout new branches (14:9). Psalm 80:11 pictures Israel as a vine whose boughs cover the mighty cedars, while Isaiah 27:11 describes dried-out branches used as firewood. The Spanish 'rama(s)' (branch/es) captures this arboreal sense precisely.

senses.1: Boughs or branches of a tree, used collectively for leafy upper growth. Spanish 'rama' / 'ramas' (branch/branches) and English 'branch' / 'boughs' confirm the arboreal meaning distinct from the harvest homonym. Job employs it figuratively: the wicked's branch withers above while roots dry below (18:16), the righteous man's branch stays fresh with dew (29:19), and a cut tree can sprout new growth (14:9). Psalm 80:11 extends Israel-as-vine whose boughs overshadow cedars, and Isaiah 27:11 pictures dried branches broken for fuel.

gloss_terse: short (of hand: feeble; of spirit: impatient; of days: short-lived)
gloss_readable: An adjective meaning 'short' that never appears alone but always in construct phrases yielding vivid figurative meanings. 'Short of hand' (2 Kings 19:26; Isaiah 37:27) describes the feebleness of nations before God. 'Short of spirit' or 'short of temper' (Proverbs 14:17,29) characterizes the impatient person, contrasted with the one 'slow to anger.' 'Short of days' (Job 14:1) captures human mortality. Spanish 'corto de' (short of) and French 'court de' mirror the Hebrew construct pattern, showing how physical shortness becomes a metaphor for limitation.

senses.1: Short—always in construct with another noun to produce figurative meanings: 'short of hand' (feeble, powerless), 'short of spirit/temper' (impatient, quick-tempered), or 'short of days' (short-lived). Spanish 'corto de' and French 'court de' replicate the Hebrew pattern of shortness-as-deficiency. In Proverbs 14:17,29 it describes the hot-tempered person, contrasted with patience; in 2 Kings 19:26 and Isaiah 37:27 it characterizes helpless nations; in Job 14:1 it laments humanity's brief lifespan.

gloss_terse: axe (a cutting tool for felling trees and clearing wood)
gloss_readable: A noun for the axe, a heavy woodcutting implement. Abimelech takes his axe to cut branches on Mount Zalmon in his assault on the tower of Shechem (Judges 9:48). In 1 Samuel 13:20–21 it appears among the farming tools the Israelites must have sharpened by the Philistines, revealing their subjugation. Psalm 74:5 pictures the enemy smashing the temple's carved woodwork with axes, and Jeremiah 46:22 compares the invading army to woodcutters advancing with axes. Spanish 'hachas' and French 'hache' preserve the same implement.

senses.1: An axe used for felling trees and chopping wood, both in literal and military contexts. Spanish 'hacha(s)' and French 'hache' consistently render this woodcutting implement. Judges 9:48 features Abimelech wielding his axe to cut branches for a siege; 1 Samuel 13:20–21 lists axes among the iron tools Israelites could not sharpen without Philistine permission; Psalm 74:5 depicts the destruction of the temple's carved panels with axes; and Jeremiah 46:22 compares Egypt's invaders to lumberjacks advancing with axes.

gloss_terse: cold, coldness (of weather, night, or winter conditions)
gloss_readable: A feminine noun denoting cold or coldness as a weather condition. Nahum 3:17 compares Nineveh's guards to locusts that settle on walls on a cold day but flee when the sun rises. Proverbs 25:20 memorably warns that singing songs to a heavy heart is like vinegar on a wound—or removing a garment on a cold day. Job 24:7 describes the destitute who have no covering against the cold of night, while Job 37:9 traces cold to the scattering winds. Psalm 147:17 asks who can withstand God's cold. Spanish 'frío' and French 'froid' uniformly confirm the meteorological sense.

senses.1: Cold or coldness as a physical weather condition—winter chill, cold nights, or frigid winds. Spanish 'frío,' French 'froid,' and English 'cold' uniformly render this atmospheric condition. Nahum 3:17 pairs it with a specific day ('a cold day'), Proverbs 25:20 uses it in a proverb about insensitivity, Job 24:7 describes exposure of the poor without shelter, Job 37:9 traces the cold to God's storehouses of wind, and Psalm 147:17 asks rhetorically who can stand before God's cold.

gloss_terse: to lay beams, furnish with beams (construction of roofs, gates, and upper chambers)
gloss_readable: A denominative Piel verb meaning to lay or set beams in place—a specialized construction term. In Nehemiah's rebuilding narrative, this verb appears three times: Nehemiah requests timber to beam the gates of the citadel (2:8), and two groups of workers 'laid its beams' while repairing Jerusalem's walls (3:3, 3:6). Second Chronicles 34:11 uses it for Josiah's temple restoration. Most strikingly, Psalm 104:3 applies it to God, who 'lays the beams' of his upper chambers on the waters—a majestic cosmological image. Spanish 'enmaderar' (to timber/beam) captures the technical carpentry meaning.

senses.1: To lay beams or furnish a structure with timber beams—a technical construction term used in the Piel stem. Spanish 'enmaderar' (to timber) precisely renders this carpentry action. Three of five occurrences cluster in Nehemiah's wall-rebuilding project (2:8; 3:3; 3:6), where teams lay beams for gates and wall sections. Second Chronicles 34:11 uses it for Josiah's temple repair. The most poetic occurrence is Psalm 104:3, where God himself 'lays the beams' of his upper chambers upon the cosmic waters.

gloss_terse: Kiriath-Sepher (ancient name of Debir, meaning 'city of the book/scribe')
gloss_readable: An ancient Canaanite place name meaning 'city of the book' or 'scribe-town,' identified as the earlier name of Debir in the southern hill country of Judah. The name appears in the narrative of Caleb's conquest, where he offers his daughter Achsah to whoever captures Kiriath-Sepher—a challenge taken up by Othniel (Joshua 15:15–16; Judges 1:11–12). Joshua 15:49 preserves the variant Kiriath-Sannah. The site is likely modern Dhahiriyye, southwest of Hebron. All four target languages transliterate the name consistently, confirming its proper-noun status.

senses.1: The proper name of an ancient Canaanite city, an earlier designation for Debir in southern Judah, meaning 'city of the book' or 'scribe-town.' All translations—Spanish 'Quiriat-Sefer,' French and German 'Kiryat-Sefer'—transliterate rather than translate, preserving its proper-noun identity. It appears in the twin conquest accounts of Joshua 15:15–16 and Judges 1:11–12, where Othniel captures it to win Achsah as his wife. Joshua 15:49 gives the alternate name Kiriath-Sannah.
